Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS): A Pediatric Case Report
N.S. Shah .1 , A. Hahn 2, B. Banwell 1. 1Toronto, Canada; 2London,
Canada
Introduction: SPS is a rare disorder characterized by fluctuating muscle
rigidity and spasms. Most patients present in adulthood. We report a case
with onset at 8 years, review of reported pediatric cases, and discuss
various therapeutic modalities.
Clinical evulation: A previously healthy, athletic 8 year old girl had onset
of severe episodes of pain in lower back and legs. Recurrent, episodic mus-
cle stiffness precipitated by loud noise and tactile stimulation lasting 3 to
5 minutes, occurred multiple times per day. Examination during episodes
revealed muscle stiffness with extreme pain with hyperreflexia. Reduced
lumbar extension and subjective stiffness in lower paraspinal muscles
without myotonia was evident between attacks. MRI head, CSF stud-
ies, evoked potentials, and electromyography (performed when asymp-
tomatic) were normal. Serum studies performed by the Mayo Clinic
demonstrated GAD-65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) antibody titres of
0.13(normal = 0.02). Serum glucose and thyroid function were normal.
Treatment: High dose corticosteroids significantly improved muscle
spasms during attacks. The frequency of attacks was markedly reduced
with monthly IVIg infusions and muscle stiffness has improved on main-
tenance regime of Tizanidine and Gabapentin.
Discussion: SPS is presumed to have an autoimmune pathogenesis, based
on presence of GAD autoantibodies and association with other autoim-
mune or paraneoplastic disorders. SPS is extremely rare in the pediatric
population. The 8 cases described in the literature will be reviewed. The
management of the present case highlights the need for multisymptomatic
therapy.
